LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- One of two doctors charged with conspiring to furnish drugs to Anna Nicole Smith before her fatal overdose in 2007 surrendered to authorities and was jailed Monday, authorities said. Anna Nicole Smith's boyfriend Howard K. Stern was among those charged last week. Dr. Khristine Eroshevich surrendered at the Van Nuys, California, jail, said police and jail officials. Bail was set at $20,000, but Eroshevich had not posted bail as of Monday afternoon. Eroshevich was charged last week along with Howard K. Stern, Smith's longtime partner and attorney; and Dr. Sandeep Kapoor. Stern and Kapoor were arrested and released from a Los Angeles County jail Thursday night after each posted a $20,000 bond. All three are charged with eight felonies, including conspiring to furnish controlled substances, unlawfully prescribing a controlled substance and obtaining fraudulent prescriptions from June 2004 through January 2007, only weeks before Smith's death. Kapoor and Eroshevich were also charged with obtaining a prescription for opiates by "fraud, deceit or misrepresentation." And each was charged with one count of obtaining a prescription for opiates by giving a false name or address, prosecutors said. "Anna was the center of a cruel tabloid feeding frenzy," Eroshevich's attorney, Adam Braun, told CNN in a statement Monday. "In the face of this, Dr. Eroshevich did her best to help the patient while protecting what little privacy Anna had left. Any actions were done with the patient's well-being in mind and were certainly not criminal." California Attorney General Jerry Brown said the doctors and Stern devised a plan to use fake names so Smith could be prescribed "thousands of pills." The former Playboy playmate and reality TV star was drugged "almost to the point of stupefaction," Brown said. "The quantity of the drugs, the variety of the drugs, the combination at any given point, and her continuing to use that -- that, to a professional, is clear evidence of addiction," Brown said Friday. "These cocktails of methadone and antidepressants and sleeping pills and Xanax, you put all that into a cocktail, it explodes and can cause death, injury and permanent morbidity and disability." Brown said Stern was the "principal enabler" in a conspiracy with two doctors for giving the "known addict" thousands of prescription pills. Stern's attorney Krista Barth said on CNN's "Larry King Live" on Friday night that she thought Brown's comments were prejudicial. "I don't think that this was something that should have been stated in a public forum," Barth said. "I think it's contrary to the rules of professional conduct regarding trial publicity. And you have to wonder why such a statement was made." Smith, 39, was pronounced dead February 8, 2007, after being found unconscious in her hotel room at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino near Hollywood, Florida. A coroner said she died from an accidental overdose of prescription drugs. Officials said that both prescription and over-the-counter drugs were found in Smith's system, including three antidepressant or anti-anxiety drugs. Human growth hormone and chloral hydrate, a sleep medication, were also found in toxicology tests, officials said. CNN's Marc Balinsky contributed to this report.

# Howard K. Stern, doctors charged in Anna Nicole Smith drug conspiracy

**By CNN Staff**  
**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Three people, including Howard K. Stern, the longtime lawyer and companion of Anna Nicole Smith, have been charged with multiple felonies in connection with the fatal drug overdose of the former Playboy model, California authorities announced Thursday.

The charges stem from an extensive investigation into the prescription drug frenzy that preceded Smith’s death at a Florida hotel in February 2007. 

In addition to Stern, California Attorney General Jerry Brown named two of Smith’s former physicians—Dr. Sandeep Kapoor and Dr. Khristine Eroshevich—in an 11-count felony complaint. The trio is accused of conspiring to furnish thousands of prescription pills to a known addict, often using false names to conceal the transactions.

"These individuals repeatedly and excessively supplied thousands of prescription pills to Anna Nicole Smith, often using fictitious names," Attorney General Brown said at a news conference in Los Angeles. "There was a system established here where excessive amounts of dangerous drugs were fed to a person who was clearly an addict."

### Excessive Prescriptions and Aliases

According to court documents, the defendants allegedly provided Smith with a toxic cocktail of opiates, sedatives, muscle relaxants, and anti-anxiety medications in the months leading up to her death. 

Investigators allege that doctors Kapoor and Eroshevich wrote prescriptions for powerful substances—including methadone, hydromorphone (Dilaudid), and vicodin—using fake names such as "Michelle Chase" and even Stern’s name to circumvent regulatory oversight. Stern is accused of acting as the facilitator, enabling the doctors and securing the drugs for Smith.

If convicted, the charges—which include conspiracy to commit a crime, obtaining controlled substances by fraud, and unlawfully prescribing controlled substances to an addict—carry maximum sentences of up to five years in state prison for each defendant.

### A Tragic Downward Spiral

Smith, a reality TV star and 1993 Playboy Playmate of the Year, was found unresponsive in her room at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino in Hollywood, Florida, on February 8, 2007. She was pronounced dead shortly after arriving at a local hospital. She was 39.

A Florida medical examiner later ruled her death an accidental drug overdose, citing a lethal combination of the sedative chloral hydrate and a array of other prescription drugs.

Smith’s death came just five months after her 20-year-old son, Daniel Wayne Smith, died in the Bahamas from a similar accidental prescription drug overdose while visiting his mother in the hospital following the birth of her daughter, Dannielynn.

### Defense Vows to Fight Charges

Attorneys representing the defendants pushed back strongly against the state’s allegations on Thursday night. 

L. Stephen Greenberg, an attorney representing Howard K. Stern, maintained that his client loved Smith deeply and was trying to protect her, relying entirely on the guidance of medical professionals.

"Howard Stern is innocent of these charges," Greenberg said in a statement. "He was not a medical doctor. He relied on doctors to care for Anna Nicole, and everything he did was to try and help her."

Lawyers for Dr. Kapoor and Dr. Eroshevich also denied wrongdoing, asserting that their clients acted in good faith to treat a high-profile patient suffering from severe physical pain and overwhelming emotional trauma following the sudden death of her son.

Authorities said all three defendants are expected to surrender to Los Angeles County law enforcement officials in the coming days for formal arraignment.

# Prosecutors File 11 Felony Counts Against Howard K. Stern and Anna Nicole Smith’s Physicians

**LOS ANGELES** — Two years after the fatal prescription drug overdose of former Playboy model and reality TV star Anna Nicole Smith, California authorities unsealed a sweeping 11-count felony indictment targeting her lawyer and partner, Howard K. Stern, alongside two of her primary physicians, Dr. Sandeep Kapoor and Dr. Khristine Eroshevich.

California Attorney General Jerry Brown and Los Angeles County District Attorney Steve Cooley announced the charges in March 2009, alleging that the trio engaged in a persistent, illegal conspiracy to supply Smith with thousands of potent prescription pills—including opiates, sedatives, and muscle relaxants—while she struggled with severe drug addiction.

Crucially, law enforcement officials emphasized that none of the defendants were charged with involuntary manslaughter or murder in connection with Smith’s death on February 8, 2007. Instead, the charges focused strictly on the fraudulent procurement and improper prescribing of controlled substances.

---

### The Exact Legal Charges

The 11 felony counts filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court cited violations of the California Health and Safety Code (HSC) and the California Penal Code (PC):

#### 1. Conspiracy to Commit a Crime (1 Count)
* **Charge:** **California Penal Code § 182(a)(1)**
* **Defendants:** Howard K. Stern, Dr. Sandeep Kapoor, Dr. Khristine Eroshevich
* **Allegation:** Conspiring together between June 2004 and January 2007 to commit crimes, specifically obtaining controlled substances by fraud and prescribing drugs to an addict.

#### 2. Prescribing/Administering Controlled Substances to an Addict (1 Count)
* **Charge:** **California Health and Safety Code § 11156**
* **Defendants:** Dr. Sandeep Kapoor, Dr. Khristine Eroshevich
* **Allegation:** Unlawfully prescribing, administering, and dispensing controlled substances (including Dilaudid, methadone, Vicodin, and Xanax) to a person known to be an addict (Smith).

#### 3. Obtaining Controlled Substances by Fraud, Deceit, or Misrepresentation (Multiple Counts)
* **Charge:** **California Health and Safety Code § 11173(a)**
* **Defendants:** Howard K. Stern, Dr. Sandeep Kapoor, Dr. Khristine Eroshevich
* **Allegation:** Repeatedly obtaining controlled substances by fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, or concealment of material facts. Prosecutors cited dozens of prescriptions written using fake names and aliases—including "Michelle Chase," "Howard K. Stern," and other pseudonyms—to hide Smith's identity from pharmacies and regulatory boards.

#### 4. Prescribing Without a Legitimate Medical Purpose (Multiple Counts)
* **Charge:** **California Health and Safety Code § 11153(a)**
* **Defendants:** Dr. Sandeep Kapoor, Dr. Khristine Eroshevich
* **Allegation:** Issuing prescriptions for powerful narcotics without a legitimate medical necessity, acting outside the usual course of professional practice, and failing to perform adequate medical exams.

---

### Core Allegations by Prosecution

According to court documents and statement by Attorney General Jerry Brown, the defendants operated as an enabling ring that fed Smith’s dependency:

* **Use of False Names:** Prosecutors detailed how Dr. Eroshevich and Dr. Kapoor wrote prescriptions under aliases to secure massive quantities of controlled substances. Stern was accused of knowingly collecting these medications and giving them to Smith.
* **Excessive Quantities:** Evidence presented showed that in the months leading up to her death, Smith was prescribed over 1,500 pills a month, including opiates (methadone, Dilaudid), benzodiazepines (Xanax, Klonopin), and sleep aids (chloral hydrate).
* **Professional Boundary Violations:** Prosecutors cited unprofessional intimacy, including photographs showing Dr. Kapoor embracing a semi-nude Smith at a public event and Dr. Eroshevich taking personal trips to the Bahamas with Smith.

---

### Defense Position

Attorneys for the defendants vigorously denied the charges:

* **Howard K. Stern:** Defense counsel argued that Stern relied entirely on the judgment of licensed medical professionals and acted only out of love and concern for Smith to protect her privacy from paparazzi.
* **Dr. Sandeep Kapoor & Dr. Khristine Eroshevich:** Defense attorneys contended that Smith suffered from chronic pain, severe anxiety, and extreme trauma following the sudden death of her 20-year-old son, Daniel, in 2006. The defense argued that using aliases for celebrity patients was a common industry practice to protect privacy and prevent theft by fans or tabloid reporters.

---

### Case Epilogue: The Verdicts and Aftermath

The trial, which concluded in October 2010, yielded mixed results and years of subsequent legal appeals:

* **Dr. Sandeep Kapoor:** Acquitted of all charges by the jury.
* **Howard K. Stern:** Found guilty by the jury on two felony counts of conspiracy/fraud for using false names on prescriptions. However, in January 2011, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Robert Perry dismissed the convictions, ruling there was insufficient evidence that Stern acted with fraudulent intent. After years of prosecution appeals, Stern's dismissal was permanently upheld in 2015.
* **Dr. Khristine Eroshevich:** Found guilty of two felony counts related to obtaining drugs via fraud. Judge Perry subsequently reduced her convictions to misdemeanors, citing her lack of prior criminal history and genuine intent to treat a patient in pain. She was sentenced to one year of probation and a $100 fine.

According to court filings, the defendants prescribed over 1,500 pills in a single month shortly before Smith’s fatal overdose in Florida at age 39. State prosecutors asserted that operating under fake names constituted felony fraud, deceit, and illegal prescription practices under California law.

Defense attorneys, however, maintained that the use of aliases was a standard, albeit informal, practice in Hollywood designed solely to protect the privacy of high-profile celebrities from paparazzi and media leaks. They argued that the defendants acted out of genuine concern for Smith’s physical pain and insomnia, rather than criminal intent.

### Outcomes and Legal Consequences

The legal proceedings yielded mixed outcomes, reflecting the complex boundary between medical malpractice, celebrity privacy, and criminal intent:

*   **Dr. Sandeep Kapoor:** The physician was acquitted of all charges after his defense demonstrated that his treatment met acceptable medical standards and that he acted in good faith without intent to defraud.
*   **Dr. Khristine Eroshevich:** Initially facing multiple felony conspiracy counts, Eroshevich was convicted of reduced misdemeanor charges related to obtaining drugs under a false name. She was sentenced to probation and ordered to pay fines, avoiding state prison time.
*   **Howard K. Stern:** Stern was initially convicted by a jury on two conspiracy counts related to using false names to obtain prescriptions. However, Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Perry subsequently dismissed the convictions, ruling that there was insufficient evidence that Stern intended to commit fraud, noting his primary motive was protecting Smith's confidentiality.

### Industry Impact and Precedent

The rulings have sent a strong signal throughout the medical and legal communities regarding the treatment of celebrity patients. Law enforcement officials emphasized that while celebrity privacy is understandable, physicians cannot violate state drug laws or use fraudulent methods to dispense controlled substances.

The case has prompted medical boards across the nation to reinforce guidelines regarding the strict prohibition of false names on prescriptions, clarifying that privacy concerns do not exempt medical professionals from federal and state controlled substance statutes. 

Smith’s death and the subsequent trials remain a definitive case study in the legal liabilities facing medical professionals and handlers operating within high-stress celebrity environments.

Dr. Khristine Eroshevich, the Los Angeles psychiatrist accused of illegally feeding Anna Nicole Smith’s lethal prescription drug habit, surrendered to authorities at the Van Nuys jail late Monday. Her booking marks the latest arrest in a sweeping criminal prosecution that California Attorney General Jerry Brown claims exposed a toxic network of celebrity enabling.

Eroshevich, 61, arrived quietly at the LAPD Van Nuys Division station, accompanied by her attorney, where she was booked on multiple felony counts before posting $20,000 bail and being released. Her surrender comes just days after criminal charges were unsealed against her, fellow physician Dr. Sandeep Kapoor, and Howard K. Stern, Smith’s longtime attorney and companion.

The arrests stem from a two-year state investigation into the events leading up to the former Playboy model's fatal drug overdose in a Florida hotel room in February 2007. 

At a stark press conference announcing the charges, Attorney General Jerry Brown did not mince words regarding the roles played by the doctors and Smith's inner circle. While Brown condemned the medical professionals for violating their Hippocratic oaths, he saved his sharpest criticism for Stern, painting him as the ringleader of a devastatingly codependent system.

Brown explicitly branded Stern the "principal enabler" in Smith’s tragic downfall, alleging that Stern actively facilitated the acquisition of thousands of powerful pills—including opiates, sedatives, and muscle relaxants—while Smith descended into severe addiction. 

"There was a system of enabling here," Brown told reporters, describing a lavish lifestyle fueled by a dangerous, illegal pipeline of pharmaceuticals. "Howard K. Stern was the principal enabler. He worked in concert with these doctors to obtain vast quantities of controlled substances for Anna Nicole Smith, often using false names and fraudulent prescriptions."

According to the 11-count felony complaint, Eroshevich—who was not only Smith’s psychiatrist but also her neighbor and friend—conspired with Kapoor and Stern to illegally furnish controlled substances to an addict. Prosecutors allege that Eroshevich prescribed excessive amounts of drugs under fictitious names, such as "Michelle Chase," to conceal Smith's identity and bypass standard medical oversight. 

Court documents detail a harrowing list of medications prescribed to the 39-year-old star in the months before her death, including Dilaudid, Vicodin, Xanax, Methadone, and chloral hydrate, a powerful sleep medication that ultimately contributed to her accidental overdose. 

Eroshevich’s defense attorney, Bradley Brunon, strongly rejected the state's characterization of his client outside the Van Nuys station on Monday, framing her actions as those of a caring friend trying to help a woman in extreme physical and emotional anguish. 

"Dr. Eroshevich was acting out of compassion, not criminality," Brunon said. "She was trying to help someone who was in terrible distress after the sudden death of her son, Daniel. This was not a case of a doctor operating a pill mill for profit. She stepped into a chaotic situation to render aid."

Brunon also pushed back against the Attorney General’s rhetoric, arguing that the state was sensationalizing the case because of Smith’s fame. "It is easy for the Attorney General to stand behind a podium and make grand claims, but when the evidence is presented in court, it will show that Dr. Eroshevich did not commit any crime," he added.

Stern, who turned himself in to authorities in Sacramento late last week before being released on bail, has also denied any wrongdoing through his legal team, maintaining that he relied entirely on the judgment of qualified physicians to treat Smith's chronic pain and sleep disorders.

For residents of Los Angeles and observers of the long-running tragedy, Eroshevich’s late-night booking at the Van Nuys jail signals that the legal reckoning over Anna Nicole Smith’s death is only just beginning.
